sources.excerpt: Publicly available generative AI (GenAI) tools are rapidly emerging, and the release of iterative versions is outpacing the adaptation of national regulatory frameworks. The absence of national regulations on GenAI in most countries leaves the data privacy of users unprotected and educational institutions largely unprepared to validate the tools. Based on a humanistic vision, the Guidance proposes key steps to the regulation of GenAI tool, including mandating the protection of data privacy, and setting an age limit for the independent conversations with GenAI platforms. To guide the proper use of the tools in education and research, this Guidance proposes a human-agent and age-appropriate approach to the ethical validation and pedagogical design processes.

sources.excerpt: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the African Union (AU) Commission renewed their longstanding strategic partnership today with the signing of an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the sidelines of the 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva. Celia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owl

It all began on a Dutch trading ship in 1628. No, really. When the Batavia set sail from Amsterdam, it crashed and the shipwrecked survivors were left stranded on a tiny island off the coast of Western Australia. As mutineers eyed the Batavia’s stash of silver, shipmates, friends and families turned on each other. About 100 people were brutally murdered, making it one of the most violent chapters in maritime history.

Nearly 400 years later, in 2015, creative entrepreneur Marc Pos had a lightbulb moment while reading about this “adult Lord of the Flies” atrocity. It gave him the idea for a reality TV show – the game of trust and treachery we now know as The Traitors . It was originally envisaged to take place on a boat, with banished players jumping overboard into the sea.

After Susan Brison was raped and left for dead, her husband, Thomas, did his best to support her. They are still together, while many relationships collapse after a sexual assault. What did he get right – and wrong?

On a hot, still, silent noon, at a junction of dirt roads in rural France , Thomas Trezise stood scanning the horizon, looking and listening for his wife. He tried to soothe a deep foreboding. Susan Brison had headed out for a morning walk two hours ago. How could she be gone so long?

This was 4 July 1990, the start of what was meant to be a busy summer. Trezise and Brison were both assistant professors in the US – he in French at Princeton and Brison in philosophy at Dartmouth – and had just arrived at the remote farmhouse of Trezise’s French colleague. Life seemed packed with promise. “I’d found someone with whom I really wanted to spend my life and I just felt very, very lucky,” says Trezise. “Susan and I had fallen quickly and deeply in love – it was magical – and at that point, we were also trying to conceive a child. We loved being in France. I kind of felt I’d found my way. It was a good place … until it happened.”

Black people are more prominent than ever in the UK’s politics and culture. But are they overwhelmingly from the middle class, as Brown argues in his new book? And if so, why isn’t anyone talking about it?

Symeon Brown and David Lammy went to the same primary school in Tottenham, north London. One went on to a selective secondary school, and became the second black person to hold one of Britain’s great offices of state. The other became a journalist who would go on to survey the country’s black professional class more thoroughly than anyone ever had – and who remembers being told by Lammy that he could “never become prime minister, because you sound like where you come from”.

It was 2010, and Brown, interested in politics, was interning for the then Labour backbencher. “And he was right, certainly at the time,” Brown says now.

sources.excerpt:
Their hopes of having a second child were dashed. Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that time

“I’m afraid this cycle has not been successful.” Emma and I cannot catch each other’s eye. We sit mute in our grief in the silence of the IVF doctor’s office. This is a kind of grief that is often not understood even to be grief at all. A grief about the loss of a potential child. An anticipatory grief – a grief for something that hasn’t yet appeared – a mourning for a possibility, of a longed-for future life to welcome, love and nurture. And there are no set grief rituals for this – for a child never present – no space in our society to mark, to grieve an actual physical death. It is a silent, achingly lonely, atomised grief. We had undergone many attempts in the years after the birth of our daughter Gaia. But that did not make this any easier.

Kenya’s biggest protest in recent history played out on a walkie-talkie app

According to Herman Manyora, a political analyst and lecturer at the University of Nairobi, mobilization had always been the greatest challenge in organizing previous protests in Kenya. Bundled up against the freezing cold, she entered the metro at the CSKA station on the Bolshaya Koltsevaya line, passing through station barriers that let travelers pay by scanning their faces.

A fake image of a Georgia mayor kissing a person went viral. Can US voters trust everything they see?

articles.explanatoryTitle: Better practice results may hide weaker learning
articles.gist: A high-school mathematics experiment compared ordinary GPT-4 assistance, a tutor with teacher-designed safeguards, and a control group. AI helped during practice, but the ordinary-assistant group later performed worse on an unassisted test. The guarded tutor largely avoided that harm. These findings concern the study’s maths setting, not all subjects or all AI tools.
evidence: The paper was published online on 25 June 2025.
The ordinary-assistant group’s unassisted exam performance was 17% lower relative to control; the guarded-tutor group was statistically indistinguishable from control.
articles.analysis: finishing a task and learning to do it independently are different outcomes. This is a useful counterexample to the claim that better assisted performance automatically means better education.
articles.limitations: A particular high-school mathematics experiment, not all subjects or tools. It did not test Study Mode. Online publication: 25 June 2025; issue date: 1 July 2025. The reported 17% is relative, not percentage points.

evidence: Publicly available generative AI (GenAI) tools are rapidly emerging, and the release of iterative versions is outpacing the adaptation of national regulatory frameworks.

evidence: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the African Union (AU) Commission renewed their longstanding strategic partnership today with the signing of an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the sidelines of the 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva.

articles.explanatoryTitle: Gender gaps in education narrow globally, yet early marriage remains a major barrier to girls’ education, new UNESCO report shows
articles.publisherHeadline: Gender gaps in education narrow globally, yet early marriage remains a major barrier to girls’ education, new UNESCO report shows

headlineVerification.observedHeading: Gender gaps in education narrow globally, yet early marriage remains a major barrier to girls’ education, new UNESCO report shows

articles.listHook: Equal enrolment does not guarantee equal educational experience.
articles.gist: UNESCO reports progress towards gender parity in school enrolment while noting that girls still face barriers in education.
articles.analysis: Newsren interpretive question: UNESCO notes parity in enrolment alongside barriers to completion and thriving. Which measure would be most revealing if access improves but outcomes remain unequal?
articles.limitations: This is UNESCO’s report account. Global averages cannot establish the situation of every country or student; publication date was not retained. Selected-passage paraphrase only, not a full-article summary. Newsren interpretation is a question, not an additional reported fact. Source assertions/figures remain attributed and as of publication; rights unconfirmed.
evidence: The world has made major progress towards gender equality in education over the past decades, with as many girls as boys now enrolled in schools from pre-primary through to secondary education.
However, too many girls still face barriers to accessing, completing and thriving in school.
Gender equality is a global priority for UNESCO, and we are mobilized with governments and partners around the world to protect girls’ right to education and expand opportunities for all.

The 2026 UNESCO Global Education Monitoring (GEM) Gender Report , published on the occasion of the International Day of the Girl Child (11 October), shows that countries around the world have made significant progress towards gender parity in education.
Nepal closed a 33-percentage-point gap in lower secondary completion between girls and boys from 1990 to 2024.

articles.listHook: A warming pathway is conditional, not a forecasted guarantee.
articles.gist: UNEP describes a conditional scenario for limiting warming overshoot and returning to 1.5°C by the end of the century.
articles.analysis: Newsren interpretive question: UNEP's pathway includes a probability and an overshoot period. How should that uncertainty change the way a return to a temperature threshold is communicated?
articles.limitations: These are conditional scenarios and UNEP’s assessment, not guaranteed temperature outcomes. Selected-passage paraphrase only, not a full-article summary. Newsren interpretation is a question, not an additional reported fact. Source assertions/figures remain attributed and as of publication; rights unconfirmed.
evidence: Nairobi, 21 October 2026 – With global temperature rise set to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions are needed to minimize the magnitude and duration of overshoot and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century, a new UNEP report finds.

The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return looks at a ‘lowest possible’ 1.5°C overshoot scenario, in which peak warming by around the middle of the century is limited to 1.7-1.8°C and global temperature rise is returned to or below 1.5°C by 2100, with about a 50 per cent chance.

evidence: In an unprecedented show of unity in support of the World Health Organization, 14 African countries and many partners pledged over US$ 45 million to the WHO Investment Round, a three-month-old initiative aimed at generating sustainable financing for the organization at the center of the global health architecture.

evidence: Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being.
At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre.

India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.

The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building.

articles.gist: In an interview, Anthony LaPaglia says he moves on quickly after missing out on acting roles rather than dwelling on disappointment.

It’s for your own mental health.
Once it’s gone, it’s gone.

articles.gist: An exhibition at SFMOMA brings together art from BTS member RM’s private collection, with the musician discussing it at a media preview.
evidence: K-pop star RM gave a boost to the previously struggling SFMOMA with an exhibition of over 100 pieces from his collection

Two years ago, RM of the wildly popular K-pop boyband BTS was serving as a soldier in the South Korean military when he received an offer from América Castillo, a museum curator in San Francisco: would he consider an exhibition of his private art collection?

“I loved it,” said RM (real name: Kim Namjoon) at the media preview of RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me , a new exhibition that opened in San Francisco earlier this month and is co-curated by SFMOMA’s Castillo and Hyoeun Kim.
“There aren’t many things that show a person more honestly than a collection they’ve built over a long period of time.”

articles.gist: The report traces the idea for The Traitors to Marc Pos reading about the Batavia shipwreck and its violent aftermath.
evidence: Celia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet.
The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owl
It all began on a Dutch trading ship in 1628.
No, really.
When the Batavia set sail from Amsterdam, it crashed and the shipwrecked survivors were left stranded on a tiny island off the coast of Western Australia.
As mutineers eyed the Batavia’s stash of silver, shipmates, friends and families turned on each other.
About 100 people were brutally murdered, making it one of the most violent chapters in maritime history.
Nearly 400 years later, in 2015, creative entrepreneur Marc Pos had a lightbulb moment while reading about this “adult Lord of the Flies” atrocity.
It gave him the idea for a reality TV show – the game of trust and treachery we now know as The Traitors .
It was originally envisaged to take place on a boat, with banished players jumping overboard into the sea.

articles.gist: DJ Jane Fitz’s request that people talk less during sets sparked a debate about behaviour on club dancefloors.
evidence: Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland.
With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should be
Towards the end of summer, a debate began raging in clubland, kick-started by an Instagram post from the esteemed DJ Jane Fitz.
Ahead of the Houghton festival, where she is a regular fixture, she posted a request asking people to stop chatting so much during DJ sets.
“What I wrote was super respectful,” she tells me.
“A bit of talking is obviously OK.
But why would you stand completely still, where the sound is super loud, just to ask your mate about a new boyfriend or what they had for lunch?
It’s called a dancefloor for a reason.”

articles.gist: The interview contrasts Sandra Hüller’s controlled screen presence with an emotional moment in person.
evidence: New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany.
She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movie
Sandra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange.
A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is.
On screen, though, she is most often asked to embody deep self-possession.
Even doing karaoke, Hüller is in control.
And in real life, life is good.
Her 2026 will end with four high-profile movies this year alone.

Two (Fatherland and Rose) are black-and-white arthouse films that centre on her brilliance, and though one of the others (Digger) is already a Hollywood cautionary tale, a second (Project Hail Mary) was a giant $684m hit. (There may also be a fifth movie, bigger still.
We will come back to that.)
And yet, dressed in film star black, she is in tears.
“This is really hard for me,” she says.

articles.gist: A research collaboration says it developed a fertile Cavendish banana, potentially allowing breeding for disease resistance.
evidence: With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain future
Love them or loathe them, bananas are one of the world’s most popular fruit .

But a combination of the climate crisis and new killer diseases have had growers concerned over the banana’s threatened extinction , something that would impose a huge toll on farmers in countries from Guatemala to Malawi, alongside eradicating a staple food.
Now researchers say they have made fresh advances in the race to save them from disaster.

This month, Yelloway – a research collaboration between Chiquita, the world’s largest banana company , and the crop-improvement company KeyGene – announced it had developed a fully fertile Cavendish banana, meaning it may be possible, through cross-breeding, to create new banana varieties that are commercially viable and resistant to disease.

articles.gist: Elon Musk raised the possibility of a Tesla–SpaceX merger but declined to add details on an earnings call.
evidence: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but declined to elaborate

Investors were paying close attention to Tesla ’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX .
But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter.
“With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX , I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call.
He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.”

articles.gist: A study found adults outperformed preschoolers on creative tasks while feeling less confident and more anxious.
evidence: Study pitting preschoolers against adults mostly in their 20s finds fear of failure and anxiety hamper the grownups
Ask a five-year-old to paint a picture and they will almost instinctively reach for the brush, but ask an adult to do the same and they will often hesitate and shy away.
Now researchers say they know why.

While it is widely assumed children are more creative than adults, a new study challenges this notion, finding adults outperform preschoolers on creative tasks but generally feel less confident and more anxious doing them.

Nothing lasts forever.
Jesse Kelly knows his meteoric rise through conservative radio will end one day – just like Donald Trump ’s power over the Republican party.

articles.gist: A US judge ordered Donald Trump to cooperate with discovery and sit for a deposition in his lawsuit against the BBC.
evidence: Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition

Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.
The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot.
The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.

The BBC will no longer have a dedicated education editor as part of a cost-cutting drive in which 100 jobs are to go across BBC News under a plan that school leaders described as “deeply regrettable”.
BBC staff have been told that the roles of education editor and social affairs editor are to be combined into a single position as part of a round of changes that will save £5.5m.

evidence: Kim Yo-jong, sister of Kim Jong-un, issues warning after inspecting border fortifications against backdrop of rising tensions

Propaganda loudspeakers aimed at South Korea will be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.

articles.gist: Protesters in French cities backed schoolchildren’s demands for teachers and building repairs while criticising policing.
evidence: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.
In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates.

They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

articles.gist: A new US rule permits hunters to bait bears with human food on federal land in Alaska, drawing environmental criticism.
evidence: Critics decry Trump administration rule that lets hunters lure bears with human foods on federal lands in Alaska

A new Trump administration rule allows hunters to bait bears on federal lands in Alaska with bacon, doughnuts, meat scraps or other human foods typically used to help kill the trophy animals at close range.
Opponents say the practice will cause bears to be more aggressive around humans, and allege that the rule change is a political gift to largely rightwing trophy hunters.
The rule replaces a 2024 Biden administration rule that banned the practice, and environmental groups criticized the move as “indefensible and inexcusable”.

evidence: Suit alleges EPA has for decades failed under the Clean Water Act to address surface-water atrazine pollution

A new lawsuit asks a federal judge to order the Trump administration to address widespread pollution from the hormone-disrupting pesticide atrazine – which has regularly been found at levels that threaten wildlife and human health.
The cancer-linked chemical is now contaminating nearly 25%, or about 860,000 miles, of all continental US rivers, according to a recent review of federal records .

evidence: New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after Deepwater Horizon disaster
Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and has still not fully recovered, according to a new study .
The April 2010 explosion of an offshore drilling unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean.

According to the study published on Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade.

articles.gist: Tim and Geli Harris fought to protect Catfield Fen. Lady Justice Lieven found that Natural England failed its statutory duty to protect the wetland from pollution.
evidence: Tim and Geli Harris have spent more than a decade fighting to protect Catfield Fen, a rare wetland in the Norfolk Broads
Polluters and regulators who fail to stop pollution must quake in their boots when they receive a letter from the lawyers for Tim and Geli Harris.

The couple, who farm 460 acres in the Norfolk Broads, have now scored a hat-trick of landmark legal victories to save an internationally important wetland after they won again in the high court this month.

Lady Justice Lieven found that Natural England failed in its statutory duty to protect Catfield Fen from pollution after nitrates and phosphates washed from arable fields into one of the finest examples of calcareous fen in western Europe, home to 2,500 species including rarities such as the fen orchid, crested buckler fern, breeding bittern and swallowtail butterflies.

articles.gist: Thomas Trezise recounts searching for Susan Brison during a 1990 visit to rural France, in an account of their experience of sexual assault.
evidence: After Susan Brison was raped and left for dead, her husband, Thomas, did his best to support her.
They are still together, while many relationships collapse after a sexual assault.
What did he get right – and wrong?
On a hot, still, silent noon, at a junction of dirt roads in rural France , Thomas Trezise stood scanning the horizon, looking and listening for his wife.
He tried to soothe a deep foreboding.
Susan Brison had headed out for a morning walk two hours ago.
How could she be gone so long?
This was 4 July 1990, the start of what was meant to be a busy summer.

Trezise and Brison were both assistant professors in the US – he in French at Princeton and Brison in philosophy at Dartmouth – and had just arrived at the remote farmhouse of Trezise’s French colleague.
Life seemed packed with promise.
“I’d found someone with whom I really wanted to spend my life and I just felt very, very lucky,” says Trezise.
“Susan and I had fallen quickly and deeply in love – it was magical – and at that point, we were also trying to conceive a child.
We loved being in France.
I kind of felt I’d found my way.
It was a good place … until it happened.”

articles.gist: Journalist Symeon Brown discusses class and opportunity in black Britain, including his experience interning for David Lammy.
evidence: Black people are more prominent than ever in the UK’s politics and culture.
But are they overwhelmingly from the middle class, as Brown argues in his new book?
And if so, why isn’t anyone talking about it?
Symeon Brown and David Lammy went to the same primary school in Tottenham, north London.
One went on to a selective secondary school, and became the second black person to hold one of Britain’s great offices of state.

The other became a journalist who would go on to survey the country’s black professional class more thoroughly than anyone ever had – and who remembers being told by Lammy that he could “never become prime minister, because you sound like where you come from”.
It was 2010, and Brown, interested in politics, was interning for the then Labour backbencher.
“And he was right, certainly at the time,” Brown says now.

articles.gist: Greg Wise describes grief following unsuccessful fertility treatment and the difficulty of seeking support.
evidence: Their hopes of having a second child were dashed.
Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that time
“I’m afraid this cycle has not been successful.”
Emma and I cannot catch each other’s eye.
We sit mute in our grief in the silence of the IVF doctor’s office.
This is a kind of grief that is often not understood even to be grief at all.
A grief about the loss of a potential child.
An anticipatory grief – a grief for something that hasn’t yet appeared – a mourning for a possibility, of a longed-for future life to welcome, love and nurture.
And there are no set grief rituals for this – for a child never present – no space in our society to mark, to grieve an actual physical death.
It is a silent, achingly lonely, atomised grief.
We had undergone many attempts in the years after the birth of our daughter Gaia.
But that did not make this any easier.

articles.gist: A Grimsby resident describes signs of change as former buildings are converted into community and leisure spaces.
evidence: Turning boarded-up shops into community spaces is a bigger and more complex task than just adding funding
“It is nice to see something happening for once,” says Jack Vincent, a Grimsby resident, as he considers a wave of change finally arriving in a town that had become a byword for deprivation.

In June, King Charles visited the Lincolnshire coastal town, celebrating the opening of a youth centre in a previously derelict Victorian warehouse building and a Care charity community drop-in centre in a vacant bank on the high street.
Scaffolding also shrouds one end of the town’s shopping centre, part of which is being converted to house leisure facilities including a cinema and a food market.

articles.gist: A father describes his anguish over children he could not save after killing an Oregon school gunman.
evidence: A father who fatally shot a gunman at his daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described his anguish over being unable to save more pupils after "hearing children pleading for their lives".
Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month.
The attacker was then killed by Kaylub Giamanco.

"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed, in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.

articles.explanatoryTitle: Phones as protest infrastructure
articles.listHook: What changes when protesters can turn phones into walkie-talkies?
articles.gist: Political analyst Herman Manyora told Rest of World that turning phones into walkie-talkies made a difference for protesters facing mobilisation challenges in Kenya.
articles.analysis: Newsren interpretive question: When does easier communication translate into a stronger public voice, rather than merely a larger mobilisation?
articles.limitations: The retained interviews attribute a mobilisation benefit to the app; they do not isolate its causal effect, establish inclusive participation, verify shared information, or prove lasting democratic improvement.
evidence: According to Herman Manyora, a political analyst and lecturer at the University of Nairobi, mobilization had always been the greatest challenge in organizing previous protests in Kenya. The ability to turn their “phones into walkie-talkies” made the difference for protesters, he told Rest of World.

“None of us saw this coming,” Moses Kemibaro, CEO of Nairobi-based digital strategy firm Dotsavvy Africa, told Rest of World. “In this instance, however, what we saw was unprecedented in terms of the scale … The young people are able to use technology in a way the older generation did not anticipate.”

articles.explanatoryTitle: Protest identification and surveillance
articles.listHook: A protester recognised a prior detention photograph on officers’ phones.
articles.gist: Rest of World reports that officers compared Zhivtsova with an image on their phones; she recognised it as a photograph from an earlier detention for protesting the war in Ukraine.
articles.analysis: Newsren interpretive question: How does the possibility of identification change the risks of joining a public protest?
articles.limitations: This retained account supports an identification and surveillance concern. It does not independently establish the technical matching process, quantify chilling effects, or prove all surveillance serves the same purpose.
evidence: On March 13, 2022, 34-year-old English teacher Yulia Zhivtsova left her Moscow apartment to meet her friends at the mall. Bundled up against the freezing cold, she entered the metro at the CSKA station on the Bolshaya Koltsevaya line, passing through station barriers that let travelers pay by scanning their faces.

The officers looked back and forth between Zhivtsova and an image on their smartphones. They seemed unsure if they had the right person. Catching a glimpse of the screen, Zhivtsova recognized a photo of herself taken the month before, when she was detained for protesting Russia’s war in Ukraine. Her hair looked different: In the photo it was faded blue, but that day it was back to a gleaming teal. “I do tend to change my hair color a lot,” Zhivtsova told Rest of World.

evidence: Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackle AI-generated fake imagery.
